decks.title: Heredity — Part 1: Variation and Mendel’s rules of inheritance
goals: Explain why sexual reproduction produces more variation than asexual reproduction
Distinguish dominant and recessive traits, and genotype and phenotype
Use a Punnett square to predict the results of monohybrid crosses
Use a Punnett square to predict the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio of a dihybrid cross

slides.heading: Heredity
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how variations build up from generation to generation, and the simple rules Mendel discovered with pea plants.

visual.alt: Flow from parents through germ cells to offspring that are similar but different

slides.narration: Namaste! Why do you have your mother’s eyes or your grandfather’s smile, yet look different from your brother or sister? The passing of traits from parents to children is called heredity. More than a hundred and fifty years ago, a monk named Gregor Mendel, working with garden peas, worked out the basic rules. Let us discover them.

slides.heading: Variation builds up over generations
slides.body_md: Every generation adds a few **new variations** from DNA copying. In **asexual** reproduction the offspring differ only by these small copying changes. **Sexual** reproduction also **mixes** DNA from two parents, so it produces **far more variation**.

rows: Copying errors plus mixing of two parents’ DNA

visual.alt: Table comparing the sources and amount of variation in asexual and sexual reproduction

slides.narration: Remember the photocopier from the last chapter. Each copy carries small slips, and those slips are passed on, so over many generations differences build up. Sexual reproduction goes further. It shuffles DNA from a mother and a father into new combinations every time. That is why children of the same parents can look so different, and why sexually reproducing species are so varied.

slides.heading: How variations accumulate
slides.body_md: Each offspring inherits its parent’s variations and adds new ones of its own, so the **diversity** of a population grows with every generation.

visual.caption: Sexual reproduction mixes the variations of two parents and creates even more diversity.

slides.narration: Follow the coloured dots down the tree. The first individual has none. Its two offspring each pick up one small new variation, shown as a blue or a green dot. In the next generation, the dots are kept and new ones appear. After just three generations, four individuals are all slightly different. Over thousands of generations, this adds up to enormous diversity.

slides.heading: Not every variation has the same chance
slides.body_md: Variations differ in how useful they are. Depending on the surroundings, some variations help an individual **survive and reproduce** more than others. Such variations become more common in the population.

visual.alt: Table showing that a heat-tolerant variation makes no difference in normal water but decides survival in heated water

slides.narration: A variation can be useful, useless or harmful, and it depends on where you live. Heat tolerance does not matter to bacteria in cool water. But in a heat wave, it decides who lives. The survivors pass the useful variation to their offspring, so over time it becomes common. The environment does not create the variation; it only selects among the variations already present.

slides.heading: Quick check: where is more variation?
slides.body_md: Why does sexual reproduction produce more variation than asexual reproduction?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about how many parents contribute DNA in each kind of reproduction.

slides.heading: Inherited traits: a closer look
slides.body_md: Children share the basic design of their parents, but details vary. Earlobes, for example, may be **free** or **attached**; both kinds are found in a population. Such features passed from parents to offspring are **inherited traits**.

slides.narration: Touch the bottom of your ear. Does the lobe hang free, or is it joined to the side of your head? Check with your classmates and your family. You will find both kinds, sometimes in the same family. Features like this are inherited, passed on through DNA. But the rules for how they pass on are not obvious. Mendel found those rules by studying simpler traits in peas.

slides.heading: Rules of inheritance: both parents count equally
slides.body_md: Both the **father** and the **mother** contribute **equal amounts** of genetic material. So for every trait, a child has **two versions** of the instruction (gene): one from each parent.

nodes.label: Father: one version of each gene
Mother: one version of each gene
Child: two versions of each gene

visual.alt: Flow: father and mother each give one version of every gene, so the child has two versions, which together decide the trait

slides.narration: Here is the first big rule. A child gets exactly half of its genetic material from the father and half from the mother. That means for every trait, such as earlobe shape or blood group, the child carries two versions of the instruction, one from each parent. The question Mendel answered was: when the two versions differ, which one shows?

slides.heading: Mendel’s pea plants
slides.body_md: Mendel crossed garden pea plants that differed in clear, **contrasting** characters, one character at a time, and **counted** the offspring.

visual.alt: Table of seven pea characters, each with two contrasting forms

slides.narration: Why peas? A pea plant has many characters that come in two clear forms, such as tall or short, and violet or white flowers. Peas grow quickly, produce many seeds, and can be cross-pollinated by hand. Mendel’s great idea was to count carefully, generation after generation. Counting turned guesswork into rules.

slides.heading: A monohybrid cross: tall × short
slides.body_md: Mendel crossed **pure tall** plants with **pure short** plants. Every plant of the first generation ($F_1$) was **tall**: no medium-height plants. When $F_1$ plants were self-pollinated, the second generation ($F_2$) had about **three tall plants for every one short**.

visual.alt: Flow of a monohybrid cross: pure tall crossed with pure short gives all tall in the first generation, and three tall to one short in the second

slides.narration: Here is the puzzle Mendel faced. The short trait vanished completely in the first generation. Every plant was tall. Yet when those tall plants were self-pollinated, short plants reappeared, about one in every four. So the instruction for shortness had not been lost. It had been hidden. Something about tallness masked it.

slides.heading: Explaining the 3 : 1 ratio with a Punnett square
slides.body_md: Let **T** be the gene version for tall and **t** for short. Pure tall is **TT**, pure short is **tt**, and every $F_1$ plant is **Tt**. Each $F_1$ parent gives **T** or **t** to a germ cell, equally often. Combining them gives **TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1**, so **3 tall : 1 short**.

visual.alt: Punnett square for crossing two Tt plants: TT, Tt, Tt and tt, so three tall to one short
visual.caption: Gametes of one parent across the top, of the other down the side.

slides.narration: A Punnett square is a simple grid for combining germ cells. Write one parent’s germ cells across the top and the other’s down the side, then fill each box. Three boxes contain at least one capital T, so those plants are tall. Only one box has two small t’s, and that plant is short. One copy of the tall version is enough to make a plant tall.

slides.heading: Dominant, recessive, genotype and phenotype
slides.body_md: A trait that shows even when only **one copy** is present is **dominant** (tall, T). A trait that shows only when **both copies** are of that kind is **recessive** (short, t). The **genotype** is the gene combination (TT, Tt, tt); the **phenotype** is the trait we see (tall or short).

rows: One of each; tall masks short

visual.alt: Table of the three genotypes TT, Tt and tt with their phenotypes

slides.narration: Two words to master: genotype and phenotype. The genotype is the pair of instructions written inside the cells. The phenotype is what you can actually see. Notice that two different genotypes, double capital T and capital T small t, give the same phenotype: tall. That is why you cannot always tell a plant’s genotype just by looking at it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: predicting numbers
slides.body_md: Two $F_1$ tall pea plants (Tt) are crossed, and **1240** $F_2$ plants grow. How many are expected to be tall and how many short? How many tall plants are expected to be pure (TT)?
bullets: Step 1 — From the Punnett square, tall $= \dfrac{3}{4}$ and short $= \dfrac{1}{4}$.
Step 2 — Tall $= \dfrac{3}{4} \times 1240 = 930$; short $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 1240 = 310$.
Step 3 — Pure tall (TT) $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 1240 = 310$, so $930 - 310 = 620$ tall plants are Tt.

visual.alt: Worked table: of 1240 plants, 310 TT, 620 Tt and 310 tt, giving 930 tall and 310 short

slides.narration: Turn the Punnett square into fractions, then multiply by the total. Three quarters of twelve hundred and forty is nine hundred and thirty tall plants, and one quarter is three hundred and ten short ones. Only a third of the tall plants are pure. Real counts will be close to these numbers, not exact, because which germ cells meet is a matter of chance.

slides.heading: Quick check: the first generation
slides.body_md: A pure-breeding violet-flowered pea is crossed with a white-flowered pea. All the first-generation plants have violet flowers. Complete the statement.
slides.narration: Your turn. If only one flower colour appears in the first generation, what does that tell you about that colour?

slides.heading: A dihybrid cross: two characters at once
slides.body_md: Mendel then followed **two** characters together. He crossed **tall plants with round seeds** (TTRR) with **short plants with wrinkled seeds** (ttrr). All $F_1$ plants were **tall with round seeds** (TtRr): tall and round are dominant.

nodes.label: Germ cells: TR, Tr, tR, tr in equal numbers

visual.alt: Flow of a dihybrid cross: tall round crossed with short wrinkled gives all tall round, whose germ cells are of four kinds

slides.narration: Next, Mendel asked a bolder question. If a plant differs in two characters, do they travel together, or separately? He crossed tall plants with round seeds and short plants with wrinkled seeds. The first generation was all tall with round seeds, as expected. The surprise came in the second generation.

slides.heading: The 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio
slides.body_md: Each $F_1$ plant forms four kinds of germ cell — **TR, Tr, tR, tr** — in equal numbers. The 16-box Punnett square gives **9 tall round : 3 tall wrinkled : 3 short round : 1 short wrinkled**. Two of these are **new combinations** not seen in either parent.

visual.alt: Sixteen-box Punnett square for crossing two TtRr plants, giving 9 tall round, 3 tall wrinkled, 3 short round and 1 short wrinkled
visual.caption: T = tall, t = short; R = round seed, r = wrinkled seed. Any box with at least one T is tall; any with at least one R has round seeds.

slides.narration: This grid looks big, but filling it is just careful bookkeeping. Count the boxes with at least one capital T and at least one capital R: there are nine, all tall with round seeds. Three are tall with wrinkled seeds, three are short with round seeds, and one is short with wrinkled seeds. Tall wrinkled and short round are brand-new combinations.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: dihybrid numbers
slides.body_md: In a dihybrid cross like the one above, **1600** $F_2$ plants are raised. Find the expected number of each type.
bullets: Step 1 — Fractions: $\dfrac{9}{16}$, $\dfrac{3}{16}$, $\dfrac{3}{16}$, $\dfrac{1}{16}$.
Step 2 — One sixteenth of 1600 is $\dfrac{1600}{16} = 100$.
Step 3 — Tall round $= 9 \times 100 = 900$; tall wrinkled $= 300$; short round $= 300$; short wrinkled $= 100$.
Check — $900 + 300 + 300 + 100 = 1600$. Tall : short $= 1200 : 400 = 3 : 1$, as in a monohybrid cross.

visual.alt: Worked table: 1600 plants split 900, 300, 300 and 100 in the ratio 9 to 3 to 3 to 1

slides.narration: Find one sixteenth of the total first; here it is one hundred. Then multiply by nine, three, three and one. Notice the neat check at the end: if you look at height alone, you still get three tall to one short. Each character behaves exactly as if the other were not there. That is the key idea of the next slide.

slides.heading: Traits are inherited independently
slides.body_md: In the dihybrid cross, **height** and **seed shape** separated and recombined freely, producing **new combinations**. So different traits are **inherited independently** of each other.

visual.alt: Table showing that two new combinations, tall wrinkled and short round, appear in the second generation

slides.narration: If tallness and round seeds were tied together, they would always travel as a pair, and we would see only the two parent types. Instead, tall wrinkled and short round plants appeared. So the gene for height and the gene for seed shape are handed on separately. Shuffling traits like this is one more way sexual reproduction creates variation.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding an unknown genotype
slides.body_md: A tall pea plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a short plant (tt). Of 100 offspring, 52 are tall and 48 are short. What is the tall plant’s genotype?
bullets: Step 1 — The short parent (tt) can only give **t**.
Step 2 — If the tall plant were **TT**, every offspring would be Tt: all tall.
Step 3 — If it were **Tt**, it would give T and t equally: half Tt (tall), half tt (short).
Conclusion — 52 : 48 is close to 1 : 1, so the tall plant is **Tt**.

visual.alt: Worked table comparing expected offspring for TT and Tt parents with the observed 52 tall and 48 short

slides.narration: This is how geneticists detect a hidden recessive gene. Cross the plant with a pure short plant, which can only contribute the short version. If any short offspring appear, the tall parent must have been carrying a hidden short version. Here almost half are short, so the tall plant is capital T small t. Always compare each possibility with the data.

slides.heading: Quick check: new combinations
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the dihybrid cross.
slides.narration: Quick check. Do new combinations really appear? And does the reason explain why?

slides.heading: Summary: variation and Mendel’s rules
bullets: Variation builds up over generations; sexual reproduction creates much more of it.
Each parent gives one version of every gene; a child has two versions.
Dominant traits show with one copy; recessive traits need two copies.
Monohybrid: $F_1$ all dominant; $F_2$ 3 : 1 (genotypes 1 : 2 : 1).
Dihybrid: $F_2$ 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, with new combinations.
Different traits are inherited independently.

visual.alt: Summary table of monohybrid and dihybrid crosses with their first and second generation results

slides.narration: Let us recap. Variation accumulates, and sexual reproduction mixes it in new ways. Each of us carries two versions of every gene, one from each parent. One dominant copy is enough to show a trait; recessive traits need two copies. Crosses give three to one for one character and nine to three to three to one for two, because traits are inherited independently.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Mendel and Punnett squares
bullets: Always write the **parents’ genotypes**, the **germ cells** and the **Punnett square**, then the ratio.
Give **both** ratios when asked: phenotype 3 : 1 and genotype 1 : 2 : 1.
Use a capital letter for the dominant version and the same small letter for the recessive one (T, t).
A recessive trait reappearing in a later generation shows it was **hidden**, not lost.
Expected numbers are approximate: real counts come close to the ratio, not exactly.
Typical 3-mark split: cross set up (1) + Punnett square (1) + ratio with conclusion (1).

rows: 3 : 1 is the phenotype ratio; genotypes are 1 : 2 : 1
Dominant means it shows with one copy

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes about Mendelian crosses with the correct ideas

slides.narration: Here is how to collect full marks. Set out a cross in clear steps: parents, germ cells, Punnett square, ratio. Say which ratio you are giving, phenotype or genotype. Do not confuse dominant with common; a dominant trait can be rare. And when a recessive trait comes back, explain that it was hidden in carriers all along.

decks.title: Heredity — Part 2: How traits are expressed, and sex determination
goals: Explain how genes control traits through proteins, using plant height as an example
Explain why each germ cell carries one chromosome of each pair
Explain sex determination in humans using X and Y chromosomes
Describe other ways in which sex is determined in some animals

slides.heading: How traits are expressed, and boy or girl?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how a gene actually makes a plant tall, why chromosomes come in pairs, and what decides whether a baby is a boy or a girl.

visual.alt: Flow from gene to protein to a chemical change to a visible trait

slides.narration: In Part 1 we used letters like capital T and small t without asking what they really are. Now we open the box. How can a stretch of DNA make a pea plant tall? And why are boys and girls born in roughly equal numbers? The answers come from genes, proteins and chromosomes.

slides.heading: Genes make proteins
slides.body_md: Cellular **DNA** carries the information for making **proteins**. A section of DNA that provides the information for **one protein** is a **gene**. Many proteins are **enzymes**, which control the chemical reactions that build the body and its features.

rows: The information store in the nucleus
A section of DNA with the information for one protein
Made using a gene’s information; does a job in the cell
A protein that speeds up a particular chemical reaction

visual.alt: Table of DNA, gene, protein and enzyme with their meanings

slides.narration: If DNA is a recipe book, a gene is one recipe in it, the recipe for one protein. Proteins are the workers of the cell. Many of them are enzymes, which make chemical reactions happen quickly. Change a recipe even slightly, and the protein it produces may work less well. That small change can show up as a different trait.

slides.heading: From gene to plant height
slides.body_md: Plant height depends on the amount of a growth **hormone**. The hormone is made with the help of an **enzyme**. If the gene for this enzyme makes an **efficient** enzyme, plenty of hormone is made and the plant grows **tall**. If the gene is altered so the enzyme is **less efficient**, less hormone is made and the plant stays **short**.

visual.alt: Two chains: gene T makes an efficient enzyme, plenty of hormone and a tall plant; altered gene t makes a less efficient enzyme, less hormone and a short plant

slides.narration: Here is the chain for pea height. A gene carries the recipe for an enzyme. The enzyme helps the plant make a growth hormone. A good enzyme means lots of hormone and a tall plant. If the gene has a small change that makes the enzyme work poorly, less hormone is made, and the plant stays short. So a gene controls a trait through the protein it makes.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: why is Tt tall?
slides.body_md: Use the gene → enzyme → hormone idea to explain why a Tt pea plant is just as tall as a TT plant, while a tt plant is short.
bullets: Step 1 — Version T makes an efficient enzyme; version t makes a less efficient one.
Step 2 — A **TT** plant makes efficient enzyme from both copies: plenty of hormone, tall.
Step 3 — A **Tt** plant still makes efficient enzyme from its one T copy, enough for plenty of hormone: tall.
Step 4 — A **tt** plant has no efficient enzyme: little hormone, short. So T is dominant over t.

visual.alt: Worked table relating genotypes TT, Tt and tt to enzyme, hormone and height

slides.narration: This links Part 1 to Part 2 beautifully. Dominance is not magic. One working copy of the gene makes enough of the efficient enzyme to produce the hormone the plant needs, so it grows tall. Only when both copies are the altered version does the plant run short of hormone. In exam answers, connect gene, enzyme, hormone and trait in that order.

slides.heading: Genes come in pairs on chromosomes
slides.body_md: Genes are carried on **chromosomes**, which are separate, independent pieces of DNA. Each body cell has **two copies of every chromosome**: one from the father and one from the mother. A germ cell gets **one chromosome from each pair**, in any combination.

slides.narration: Our genes are not one long string. They are packed into separate pieces called chromosomes, and body cells have each chromosome in a pair. When germ cells are made, each takes just one member of every pair. Which member goes into which germ cell is a matter of chance, so from only two pairs, four different kinds of germ cell can be formed.

slides.heading: Quick check: what goes into a germ cell?
slides.body_md: A body cell has 8 chromosomes in 4 pairs. What does each of its germ cells receive?
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember that a germ cell gets one member of every pair, not a whole pair and not a random handful.

slides.heading: Chromosomes explain Mendel’s results
slides.body_md: Because each germ cell gets **one** version of each gene, $F_1$ Tt plants make **T** and **t** germ cells equally, giving 3 : 1. Because genes for different characters can lie on **different chromosomes** that sort **independently**, two characters recombine freely, giving 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

A germ cell gets one chromosome of each pair
The t version is carried on a chromosome even when not shown
New combinations in a dihybrid cross
Different chromosome pairs sort into germ cells independently

visual.alt: Table linking three of Mendel’s observations to their explanation in terms of chromosomes

slides.narration: Mendel never saw a chromosome. Yet his rules match exactly what chromosomes do. One member of each pair in every germ cell explains why each parent passes on just one version of a gene. Pairs sorting independently explains why height and seed shape mix freely. Science is wonderful when a pattern seen in numbers turns out to have a physical cause.

slides.heading: How is sex decided? Different strategies
slides.body_md: Different species decide the sex of their young in different ways. In some animals, the **temperature** at which fertilised eggs are kept decides whether they develop into males or females. In others, such as **snails**, individuals can **change sex**. In **humans**, sex is decided **genetically**.

rows: Some reptiles, such as many turtles
Temperature at which the eggs develop

visual.alt: Table of three ways sex is decided: egg temperature in some reptiles, sex change in snails, and genes in humans

slides.narration: Nature has more than one way to decide boy or girl. On the beaches of Odisha, where olive ridley turtles nest, the warmth of the sand helps decide whether hatchlings are male or female. Some snails can even change sex during their lives. In humans, though, the answer lies in our chromosomes, decided at the very moment of fertilisation.

slides.heading: Human sex chromosomes
slides.body_md: Human body cells have **23 pairs** of chromosomes. **22 pairs** (autosomes) are alike in men and women. The **sex chromosomes** differ: women have a perfect pair, **XX**; men have a mismatched pair, **XY**, with a shorter **Y**.

slides.narration: Look at the sex chromosomes. A woman’s pair matches: two X chromosomes. A man’s pair does not: one X and one smaller Y. The other twenty-two pairs are alike in everyone. Because a woman has only X chromosomes, every egg carries an X. A man’s sperms are of two kinds: half carry an X and half carry a Y.

slides.heading: Who decides: boy or girl?
slides.body_md: Every **egg** carries an **X**. If the egg is fertilised by a sperm carrying **X**, the child is **XX: a girl**. If the sperm carries **Y**, the child is **XY: a boy**. So the sex of the child depends on the **father’s** sperm, and the chance is **half and half**.

visual.alt: Punnett square for sex determination: half the combinations are XX (girl) and half XY (boy)

slides.narration: Fill in this small Punnett square and the answer jumps out. The mother can only give an X. The father gives either an X or a Y, by chance. An X from the father makes a girl; a Y makes a boy. Two of the four boxes are girls and two are boys, so each birth has an equal chance of being a boy or a girl.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: chance and families
slides.body_md: The Sharma family has three daughters. A relative says the fourth child is "sure to be a boy" this time. Is this correct? What is the chance that the fourth child is a boy?
bullets: Step 1 — Each child’s sex is decided separately, by whether the sperm that fertilises the egg carries X or Y.
Step 2 — Half the sperms carry X and half carry Y, so the chance of a boy is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for **every** birth.
Step 3 — Earlier births do not change this chance; sperms have no memory of previous children.
Conclusion — the relative is wrong: the chance of a boy is still one in two, exactly as for the first child.

visual.alt: Worked table showing the chance of a boy or a girl is one half at every birth

slides.narration: Many people believe that after several girls a boy is due, like waiting for your turn in a queue. Biology does not work that way. Each birth is a fresh event, like a fresh toss of a coin. The chance is one in two every time. Understanding this also clears up an unfair myth: the mother cannot be blamed for the sex of a child.

It is the sperm, carrying either an X or a Y, that decides, and nobody chooses which sperm reaches the egg. Every child, girl or boy, inherits half of its chromosomes from each parent.

sections.heading: 1. Accumulation of variation
sections.body_md:
Each generation inherits the basic body design of the previous one, together with **small changes** arising from DNA copying. These variations are passed on and **accumulate**, so a population becomes more diverse over generations.

- **Asexual reproduction:** offspring differ only by the small changes from DNA copying, so variation is **minimal**.
- **Sexual reproduction:** DNA from **two parents** is combined in new ways in every offspring, so it produces **much greater diversity**.

Not all variations are equally useful. Depending on the environment, some variations help individuals survive and reproduce better (for example, heat-tolerant bacteria in water that warms up). The environment **selects** among variations that already exist.

key_terms.definition_md: The passing of traits from parents to offspring.
Differences between individuals of the same species.

sections.heading: 2. Inherited traits and the rules of inheritance
sections.body_md:
Offspring share the basic features of their parents but differ in details. Earlobes, for example, may be **free** or **attached**; both forms are found in human populations.

Rules of inheritance:
- **Both parents contribute equal amounts** of genetic material to the child.
- So for each trait, a child has **two versions** of the gene: one from the father and one from the mother.
- When the two versions differ, the one that shows is **dominant**; the one that is hidden is **recessive**.

The **genotype** is the combination of gene versions (TT, Tt or tt); the **phenotype** is the trait seen (tall or short).

key_terms.definition_md: A trait that is expressed when only one copy of its gene version is present.
A trait expressed only when both copies are of that version.
The gene combination of an organism, e.g. Tt.

sections.heading: 3. Mendel’s monohybrid cross
sections.body_md:
Gregor Mendel worked with garden peas, which show clear **contrasting characters** (tall/short plants, round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds, violet/white flowers and others).

**Cross:** pure tall (TT) × pure short (tt) → $F_1$: all **tall** (Tt), no medium plants.
**$F_1$ self-pollinated:** germ cells T and t in equal numbers → $F_2$: TT : Tt : tt = **1 : 2 : 1** (genotype), **3 tall : 1 short** (phenotype).

Conclusions: a single copy of T is enough to make a plant tall (T is dominant); the short trait was hidden in $F_1$, not lost, and reappeared in $F_2$.

key_terms.definition_md: A cross that follows one pair of contrasting characters.
A grid used to combine the germ cells of two parents and predict offspring.

visual.alt: Punnett square for crossing two Tt plants: TT, Tt, Tt and tt, so three tall to one short
visual.caption: Gametes of one parent across the top, of the other down the side.

sections.heading: 4. Mendel’s dihybrid cross
sections.body_md:
**Cross:** tall plants with round seeds (TTRR) × short plants with wrinkled seeds (ttrr) → $F_1$: all **tall, round** (TtRr).

$F_1$ plants form four kinds of germ cell — **TR, Tr, tR, tr** — in equal numbers. In $F_2$: **9 tall round : 3 tall wrinkled : 3 short round : 1 short wrinkled**.

Two **new combinations** (tall wrinkled, short round) appear, so the traits for height and seed shape are **inherited independently**. Looking at one character alone still gives 3 : 1 (for example 12 tall : 4 short).

key_terms.definition_md: A cross that follows two pairs of contrasting characters at once.
Different traits are passed on separately, so they can appear in new combinations.

sections.heading: 5. How traits are expressed
sections.body_md:
Cellular **DNA** is the information source for making **proteins**. A section of DNA that provides the information for one protein is a **gene**.

**Plant height:** height depends on the amount of a particular plant **hormone**. The amount of hormone depends on how **efficient** the **enzyme** that makes it is. An efficient enzyme (from gene version T) makes plenty of hormone → **tall** plant. If the gene is altered so that the enzyme is less efficient (version t), less hormone is made → **short** plant. One efficient copy (Tt) is enough for a tall plant, which is why tall is dominant.

So **genes control traits** through the proteins they make.

key_terms.definition_md: A section of DNA that carries the information for making one protein.
A protein that speeds up a particular chemical reaction in the cell.

visual.alt: Flow from gene to enzyme to hormone to plant height

sections.heading: 6. Chromosomes and germ cells
sections.body_md:
Genes are carried on **chromosomes**, which are separate, independent pieces of DNA. Each body cell has **two copies of each chromosome**, one from each parent. When germ cells are made, each receives **one chromosome from each pair**, which may be the one from the father or the one from the mother. When two germ cells fuse, the zygote again has two copies of each chromosome.

This explains Mendel’s rules: each parent passes on one version of each gene, and chromosome pairs sort independently, so traits on different chromosomes are inherited independently.

key_terms.definition_md: A thread-like structure in the nucleus made of DNA, carrying many genes.

sections.heading: 7. Sex determination
sections.body_md:
Different species use different strategies. In some animals, such as many **reptiles**, the **temperature** at which fertilised eggs develop decides whether the young are male or female. In some animals, such as **snails**, individuals can **change sex**. In **humans**, sex is determined **genetically**.

Human body cells have **23 pairs** of chromosomes: **22 pairs of autosomes** (alike in both sexes) and **one pair of sex chromosomes** — **XX** in women and **XY** in men (Y is shorter). Every egg carries an X. Half the sperms carry X and half carry Y. Egg + X sperm → **XX, girl**; egg + Y sperm → **XY, boy**. So the **father’s sperm decides** the sex, and the chance of a boy or a girl is **one half** at each birth.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing $F_1$ tall plants as TT (they are Tt).
- Calling 3 : 1 the genotype ratio (it is the phenotype ratio; genotypes are 1 : 2 : 1).
- Thinking "dominant" means "more common".
- Leaving out the enzyme and hormone when explaining how a gene controls height.
- Saying the mother decides the sex of the child, or that a boy is "due" after several girls.
- Forgetting that germ cells carry one chromosome of each pair (23 in humans).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, term, ratio or number.
- 2–3-mark answers: cross set out with genotypes (1) + Punnett square or germ cells (1) + ratio or conclusion (1).
- 5-mark answers: full cross through $F_2$ with Punnett square (2–3) + ratios (1) + conclusion such as dominance or independent inheritance (1).
- Case-based items: two 1-mark parts from data and a 2-mark explanation or evaluation with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Why does sexual reproduction produce more variation than asexual reproduction?

options.text_md: DNA is copied more carelessly in sexual reproduction.
The environment changes the DNA of sexually produced offspring.
Asexual reproduction does not involve copying DNA at all.
It combines DNA from two parents in new ways, in addition to small copying changes.

questions.solution_md: Both kinds of reproduction involve slightly inaccurate DNA copying, but sexual reproduction also mixes DNA from two parents, giving new combinations — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A banana plantation was raised from suckers of a single plant, while a mango orchard nearby was raised from seeds collected from many trees. Which shows more variation among its plants, and why?

options.text_md: The banana plantation, because suckers grow faster
The mango orchard, because each seed came from sexual reproduction that mixes DNA from two parents
The banana plantation, because DNA copying is less accurate in suckers
Neither, because all plants of one kind are identical

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Suckers are vegetative copies of one plant: only tiny copying differences.

Step 2 — Seeds come from sexual reproduction, combining DNA of two parents in new ways, so the orchard varies more — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A farmer sprayed the same pesticide on his cotton crop every season. At first it killed almost all the insect pests; after some years it killed only a few. What is the best explanation?

options.text_md: The insects learnt to avoid the pesticide and taught their young.
The pesticide made every insect develop resistance on purpose.
A few insects already had a variation that helped them survive the pesticide, and their offspring inherited it.
The pesticide slowly lost its strength in the bottle.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — In a large population, a few insects happened to carry a variation that let them survive.

Step 2 — Each spraying killed the others; the survivors reproduced and passed the variation on, so it became common — option (c).

Step 3 — Variations are not produced on purpose (b), and learnt behaviour is not passed on through DNA (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sexual reproduction produces more variation than asexual reproduction.

**Reason (R):** In sexual reproduction, DNA from two parents is combined in the offspring.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and combining DNA from two parents is the reason for the extra variation — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Offspring produced by asexual reproduction show only very small variations.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Their only differences come from small inaccuracies in DNA copying.

questions.stem_md: How do variations arise in (a) asexual reproduction and (b) sexual reproduction? Which produces more variation?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In asexual reproduction, variations arise only from **small inaccuracies in DNA copying**.

(b) In sexual reproduction, besides copying errors, **DNA from two parents is combined** in new ways in each offspring. So **sexual reproduction** produces much more variation.

questions.solution_md: Name the source of variation in each, then compare.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Mixing of two parents’ DNA; sexual gives more

questions.stem_md: A student says, "Variations are always harmful, because they make offspring different from their well-adapted parents." Evaluate this claim, giving an example.

answer.model_answer_md: The claim is **not correct**. Many variations are harmless, and a few can be **useful**, depending on the surroundings. For example, if a pond warms up in a heat wave, the few bacteria that happen to tolerate heat survive and multiply, while the rest die. Without such variation the whole population could be wiped out. So variation helps a species **survive changes** in its environment, even though large changes in body design may be harmful.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — State whether the claim holds.

Step 2 — Give an example of a useful variation.

Step 3 — Conclude about survival of the species.

marking_scheme.step: Suitable example of a useful variation
Links variation to survival when conditions change

questions.stem_md:
(a) Why does sexual reproduction create more variation than asexual reproduction?

(b) State the rules Mendel’s work shows about how much genetic material each parent contributes, and how many versions of each gene a child has.

(c) Explain, with an example, why some variations become more common in a population over time.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Asexual offspring differ only by small DNA copying errors. In sexual reproduction, DNA from **two parents** is combined in new ways in every offspring, in addition to copying errors, so there is far more variation.

(b) Both parents contribute **equal amounts** of genetic material. So for every trait the child has **two versions** of the gene, one from the father and one from the mother; when they differ, the dominant one is expressed.

(c) Variations differ in how useful they are in a given environment. For example, when a pesticide is used year after year, the few insects that carry a variation allowing them to survive reproduce and pass it on, while the others die. Over generations the variation becomes **common**. The environment does not create the variation; it selects among existing ones.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Compare the sources of variation.

Step 2 — Equal contribution; two versions per trait.
Step 3 — Selection of an existing useful variation, with an example.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Equal contribution and two versions per trait
(c) Selection of a useful variation, with an example

questions.stem_md: When pure-breeding tall and pure-breeding short pea plants are crossed, all the first-generation plants are tall. Tallness is therefore:

options.text_md: recessive
dominant
a new variation
an acquired trait

questions.solution_md: The trait that shows in all first-generation plants, masking the other, is dominant — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure short plant (tt). What is the genotype of the first-generation plants?

options.text_md: TT
Tt
tt
A mixture of TT and tt

questions.solution_md: Every germ cell of the TT parent carries T and every germ cell of the tt parent carries t, so all offspring are Tt — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the second generation of Mendel’s tall × short cross, what is the ratio of tall plants to short plants?
questions.solution_md: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt: three tall to one short — option (a). 1 : 2 : 1 (c) is the genotype ratio.

questions.stem_md: Which two genotypes have the same phenotype in pea plants, where T (tall) is dominant over t (short)?

options.text_md: Tt and tt
TT and tt
All three, TT, Tt and tt
TT and Tt

questions.solution_md: TT and Tt both contain at least one T, so both are tall — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A tall pea plant is crossed with a short plant (tt). All 60 offspring are tall. What is the most likely genotype of the tall parent?

options.text_md: Tt
tt
It cannot be predicted at all
TT

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — The short parent gives only t.

Step 2 — A Tt parent would give t in half its germ cells, producing about 30 short offspring; none appeared.

Step 3 — So the tall parent gives only T: it is TT — option (d).

questions.stem_md: How many different kinds of germ cell can a pea plant with genotype TtRr produce?
questions.solution_md: Each germ cell gets one version of each gene: TR, Tr, tR or tr — four kinds — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the second generation of a dihybrid cross, the four phenotypes appear in the ratio:
questions.solution_md: A TtRr × TtRr cross gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Pure tall plants with round seeds are crossed with pure short plants with wrinkled seeds, and the first generation is self-pollinated. Which second-generation plants show new combinations not seen in either original parent?

options.text_md: Tall plants with round seeds only
Short plants with wrinkled seeds only
Tall plants with wrinkled seeds, and short plants with round seeds
Medium-height plants with medium seeds

questions.solution_md: The parents were tall round and short wrinkled. Tall wrinkled and short round are new combinations — option (c). There are no medium plants (d).

questions.stem_md: Two violet-flowered pea plants are crossed, and about a quarter of their offspring have white flowers. What can you conclude?

options.text_md: White is dominant, and both parents are pure violet.
White is recessive, and both parents carry one hidden version for white.
The white flowers are caused by poor soil, not by genes.
Only one parent carries the version for white.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — White appears though neither parent is white, so white was hidden: it is recessive.

Step 2 — A white plant needs two white versions, one from each parent, so both parents are hybrids (Vv); Vv × Vv gives one quarter white — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In peas, yellow seed colour (Y) is dominant over green (y). What offspring are expected when a Yy plant is crossed with a yy plant?

options.text_md: All yellow
Three yellow to one green
About half yellow and half green
All green

questions.solution_md: Yy gives Y and y equally; yy gives only y. Offspring: Yy (yellow) and yy (green) in equal numbers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two Tt pea plants are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are expected to be tall plants that will always breed true (give only tall offspring when self-pollinated)?
questions.solution_md: Only TT plants breed true. TT is one box out of four in the Punnett square — option (d). 3/4 (a) counts all tall plants, including Tt.

questions.stem_md: In the second generation of a dihybrid cross (TtRr × TtRr), 800 plants are raised. How many of them are expected to be tall, whatever their seed shape?
questions.solution_md: Tall plants are 9/16 (tall round) + 3/16 (tall wrinkled) = 12/16 = 3/4 of the total, so $\dfrac{3}{4} \times 800 = 600$ — option (c). 450 (a) counts only tall round.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A dominant trait is always more common in a population than the recessive trait.

**Reason (R):** A dominant trait is expressed even when only one copy of its gene version is present.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: "dominant" describes how a trait is expressed, not how common it is. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When pure tall and pure short pea plants are crossed, all the first-generation plants are tall.

**Reason (R):** The first-generation plants have two copies of the version for tallness (TT).

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the first-generation plants are Tt; one copy of T is enough to make them tall — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the second generation of a dihybrid cross, tall plants with wrinkled seeds and short plants with round seeds appear.

**Reason (R):** The traits for height and seed shape are inherited independently of each other.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Because the two traits are inherited independently, they recombine to give the new combinations — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A pea plant with genotype Tt is tall.

**Reason (R):** A pea plant with genotype tt produces only germ cells carrying t.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the germ cells of a tt plant say nothing about why a Tt plant is tall; that is because T is dominant — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A trait that appears in all the first-generation offspring when two pure-breeding plants with contrasting traits are crossed is called a ___ trait.
questions.solution_md: It is the **dominant** trait; the hidden one is recessive.

questions.stem_md: The visible trait of an organism, such as tall or short, is its ___, while its gene combination, such as Tt, is its ___.
questions.solution_md: **Phenotype** is what we see; **genotype** is the gene combination.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the second generation of a monohybrid cross, all the tall plants have the same genotype.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. One third of the tall plants are TT and two thirds are Tt.

questions.stem_md: Match each term in Column A with its meaning or example in Column B.

options.text_md: Genotype
Phenotype
Dominant
Recessive

match_right.text_md: Expressed with only one copy present
Expressed only when both copies are present

questions.stem_md: Two Tt pea plants are crossed and 840 offspring are raised. How many are expected to be short?
questions.solution_md: Short plants (tt) are $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the offspring: $\dfrac{1}{4} \times 840 = 210$.

questions.stem_md: Two Tt pea plants are crossed and 960 offspring are raised. How many are expected to have the genotype Tt?
questions.solution_md: Tt is 2 out of 4 boxes $= \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 960 = 480$.

questions.solution_md: Green wrinkled is 1 box out of 16: $\dfrac{1120}{16} = 70$.

|---|---|---|
| **R** | RR | Rr |
| **r** | Rr | rr |

answer.model_answer_md: The first-generation plants were **Tt**: the version for shortness was present but **hidden**, because T is dominant. When these plants were self-pollinated, each made t germ cells as well as T germ cells, and when two t germ cells combined (**tt**), about one plant in four was short.

tt combination appears in about a quarter of the second generation

questions.stem_md:
A pea plant with genotype TtRr (tall, round seeds) is self-pollinated.

(a) List the kinds of germ cell it forms.

(b) Give the four phenotypes expected in the offspring, with their ratio.

(c) What does the appearance of tall wrinkled and short round plants show?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **TR, Tr, tR, tr**, in equal numbers.

(b) Tall round : tall wrinkled : short round : short wrinkled = **9 : 3 : 3 : 1**.

(c) Height and seed shape are **inherited independently**, so they can appear in new combinations.

Step 1 — Combine one version of each gene.

Step 2 — Use the 16-box Punnett square.

questions.stem_md: A seed company has a tall pea plant and needs to know whether it is TT or Tt before using its seeds. Describe a cross that would tell them, and the results expected in each case.

answer.model_answer_md:
Cross the tall plant with a **short (tt)** plant, which can only give t germ cells.

- If the tall plant is **TT**, all its germ cells carry T, so **all offspring are tall** (Tt).
- If it is **Tt**, half its germ cells carry t, so about **half the offspring are tall and half short**.

So the appearance of any short offspring shows that the plant is Tt.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Use a short plant, which reveals the tall plant’s germ cells.

Step 2 — Predict the offspring for TT and for Tt.

Step 3 — State how to decide.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Mendel crossed pure tall pea plants with pure short pea plants. Using T and t, show the cross up to the second generation with a Punnett square.

(b) Give the phenotype and genotype ratios of the second generation.

(c) What did this cross tell Mendel about dominant and recessive traits?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Parents: TT (tall) × tt (short). Germ cells: T and t. First generation: all **Tt**, tall. First generation self-pollinated: germ cells T and t from each parent.

| | T | t |
|---|---|---|
| **T** | TT | Tt |
| **t** | Tt | tt |

(b) Phenotype: **3 tall : 1 short**. Genotype: **1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt**.

(c) A single copy of T is enough to make a plant tall, so tallness is **dominant**; shortness shows only in tt plants, so it is **recessive**. The recessive trait was **hidden**, not lost, in the first generation, and both parents contribute one version of each gene.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Set out parents, germ cells, first generation and the Punnett square.

Step 2 — Read off both ratios.

Step 3 — State the conclusions about dominance.

questions.stem_md:
In peas, yellow seed colour (Y) is dominant over green (y), and round seed shape (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r). A pure yellow round plant is crossed with a pure green wrinkled plant.

(a) What are the genotype and phenotype of the first generation?

(b) Draw a Punnett square for the second generation and give the phenotype ratio.

(c) If 640 second-generation seeds are collected, how many of each type are expected?

(d) What does this cross show about the inheritance of two traits?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **YyRr**: yellow, round.

(b) Germ cells of each parent: YR, Yr, yR, yr.

| | YR | Yr | yR | yr |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **YR** | YYRR | YYRr | YyRR | YyRr |
| **Yr** | YYRr | YYrr | YyRr | Yyrr |
| **yR** | YyRR | YyRr | yyRR | yyRr |
| **yr** | YyRr | Yyrr | yyRr | yyrr |

Yellow round : yellow wrinkled : green round : green wrinkled = **9 : 3 : 3 : 1**.

(c) One sixteenth of 640 is 40: yellow round **360**, yellow wrinkled **120**, green round **120**, green wrinkled **40**.

(d) Seed colour and seed shape are **inherited independently**; new combinations (yellow wrinkled, green round) appear.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — The first generation is YyRr.

Step 2 — Four germ cells each; 16 boxes; count phenotypes.

Step 3 — $\dfrac{640}{16} = 40$; multiply by 9, 3, 3 and 1.

Step 4 — New combinations show independent inheritance.

questions.stem_md: A gene is best described as:

options.text_md: a whole chromosome
a section of DNA that carries the information for making one protein
a protein that controls a trait
a cell that carries traits from parents

questions.solution_md: A gene is a section of DNA providing the information for one protein — option (b). It is part of a chromosome (a), not a protein (c) or a cell (d).

questions.stem_md: A pea plant carries two copies of a gene version that makes a poorly working enzyme for producing a growth hormone. The plant is most likely to be:

options.text_md: short, because it makes too little growth hormone
tall, because it has two copies of the gene
tall, because enzymes are not needed for growth
short, because the gene itself stops the stem from growing

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Both copies give a poor enzyme, so little growth hormone is made.

Step 2 — Less hormone means less growth: a short plant — option (a). The gene acts through the enzyme and hormone, not directly (d).

questions.stem_md: A body cell of an organism has 8 chromosomes in 4 pairs. What does each of its germ cells receive?

options.text_md: 8 chromosomes, both members of every pair
4 chromosomes, all from the father
2 complete pairs of chromosomes
4 chromosomes, one from each pair

children.stem_md: What is the genotype of plant B? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: **Tt**, because about half its offspring (24 of 50) were short.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain why crossing a tall plant with a short plant reveals whether the tall plant is TT or Tt.

answer.model_answer_md: The short plant (tt) can only give **t**. So each offspring’s phenotype shows the germ cell it got from the tall plant: T gives a tall offspring and t gives a short one. A **TT** plant gives only T, so all offspring are tall; a **Tt** plant gives T and t equally, so about half are short.

children.solution_md: The tt parent "reveals" the other parent’s germ cells.

marking_scheme.step: Offspring reveal TT (all tall) or Tt (half short)

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): A manager worries that plant C might still be Tt, since only 51 offspring were checked. Evaluate this worry.

answer.model_answer_md: The worry is **very unlikely** to be correct. If C were Tt, each offspring would have a one-in-two chance of being short, so we would expect about 25 short plants out of 51. Getting **none at all** by chance would be extremely unlikely. So C is almost certainly TT, though testing more offspring would make the company even more confident.

alternatives.solution_md: Compare the expected number of short offspring for Tt with the zero observed.

marking_scheme.step: Expected about half short if Tt
